title: Saying goodbye and wishing well
title_target: ជម្រាបលា និង សូមអោយ — chum-riep lie neng soum-'aoy
goal: Part ways, congratulate, and give good wishes — three things that close every relationship in Cambodia, and that decide whether you're remembered as a guest or as a stranger passing through.
bekal: say goodbye at the right level for the situation
give good wishes with the pattern សូមអោយ …
offer congratulations on holidays and happy occasions
keep relationships alive with goodbyes that leave the door open
say a thank-you that goes beyond អរគុណ

dialogs.title: កិច្ចសន្ទនា — A year later, at the airport
dialogs.intro: A year has passed. Ani is heading home to Indonesia. Sokha, Sreymom, and their mother see her off at Phnom Penh Airport. This is the last dialogue in the book — and almost every sentence uses something you've learned in the nineteen units before it.

grammars.title: ⚠️ ជម្រាបលា is too heavy for everyday goodbyes
body: Textbooks teach ជម្រាបលា as "goodbye", and beginners use it every time they part. But it is actually a **formal, distant farewell** — for long departures, speeches, or people you deeply respect. Saying it to a friend you'll see tomorrow sounds like goodbye forever.

head: Khmer
Say it
When to use it
rows: ជួបគ្នាថ្ងៃក្រោយ
"see you another day" — warm, most common
ជួបគ្នាស្អែក
"I'll head off first" — when you're the one leaving
ទៅដោយសុវត្ថិភាព
"I'll take my leave" — polite, leaving a gathering

after: ⚠️ Look at the last lines of the dialogue: Sokha **corrects** ជម្រាបលា to ជួបគ្នាថ្ងៃក្រោយ. It isn't a grammar correction but a correction of feeling — he refuses a farewell that sounds too final. A phrase that opens the door is always more appreciated than one that closes it.

grammars.title: សូមអោយ … — the pattern for good wishes
body: Wishing others well is an important part of Cambodian courtesy, and one pattern produces them all: **សូមអោយ + who + what you wish**. Literally "please let …".

head: Khmer
Say it
Meaning
rows: សូមអោយមានសុខភាពល្អ
សូមអោយធ្វើដំណើរដោយសុវត្ថិភាព
សូមអោយជោគជ័យ
សូមអោយសប្បាយរីករាយ
សូមអោយឆាប់ជា
សូមអោយមានសំណាងល្អ

after: អោយ (*'aoy*), which you know as "give" from Unit 12, here means "so that, let". It's a very busy word in Khmer, and all three of its meanings — give, so that, make — grow from the idea of handing something over.

⚠️ Notice **ជោគជ័យ** (*chook-chey*, success): ជ័យ is the Sanskrit *jaya*, "victory", which you may know from names all over South and Southeast Asia. Likewise **សំណាង** (luck) and **សុខភាព** (health, containing *sukha*). The book closes with words that came to Khmer from India, like so many before them.

grammars.title: Congratulations
body: For holidays and happy occasions, Khmer uses សួស្តី (the same word as "hello"), which means "well-being, prosperity" — so one word covers both greeting someone and wishing them well.

head: English
Khmer
Say it
rows: សួស្តីឆ្នាំថ្មី
រីករាយថ្ងៃកំណើត
សូមអបអរសាទរអាពាហ៍ពិពាហ៍
អញ្ជើញញ៉ាំបាយ
រាត្រីសួស្តី

after: ⚠️ **អញ្ជើញញ៉ាំបាយ** isn't "enjoy your meal" like *bon appétit* but **"please eat"** — said by the host to the guests, not the other way around. If you're the guest, answer អរគុណ, then start eating after the oldest person at the table has begun.

sections.title: A thank-you that goes beyond អរគុណ

blocks.text: អរគុណ on its own is always correct, but for great kindness Cambodians say something more. These sentences close a relationship warmly — and you can already build all of them from what you've learned.

blocks.title: What you're really taking home
items: **These twenty units have given you about six hundred words and the whole backbone of A1 grammar.** That's enough for everyday life: shopping, ordering, asking the way, seeing a doctor, telling stories, saying no, and saying goodbye.
**What no book can give you is the courage to say it out loud.** Cambodians almost never laugh at a foreigner who tries — instead, they stop whatever they're doing to listen.

**And one last thing to keep.** Throughout this book Khmer has kept handing you words from Sanskrit and Pali — ភាសា, មនុស្ស, គ្រូ, សិស្ស, ចិត្ត, ជីវិត, កាល, ជ័យ — the same classical languages that gave English *guru*, *karma*, and *nirvana*. You haven't been learning a wholly foreign language. You've been visiting another branch of a story that stretches across half the world.
